Equality Utah-backed candidates win or lead in 36 of 41 races; all Republican endorsees lose

StaffNovember 10, 2026
3 minutes read
% buffered00:00
00:00

Results are unofficial. Counties will certify them after the Nov. 23 canvass.

Among the GOP losses in the nationwide “Blue Wave” are the four Republicans Equality Utah endorsed this year. Utah had the largest shift toward Democrats in the nation, about 30 percentage points since 2022. Utah Republicans lost 16 House seats and their supermajority in that chamber for the first time in around three decades.

Candidates endorsed by Equality Utah’s Political Action Committee won or led in 36 of the 41 races where the group made endorsements, according to unofficial results updated Tuesday.

All four Republican endorsees lost: Rep. Anthony Loubet, Chris McConnehey, Mike Bird and Nicole McDermott. Three lost to Democrats and one to an unaffiliated candidate. All 30 Democratic endorsees won or are currently leading in the unofficial results.

Eight of the 41 endorsees had no competitor on the ballot: Sen. Stephanie Pitcher, Rep. Stephen Otterstrom, Rep. Julie Jackson, Rep. Andrew Stoddard, Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman, State Board of Education member Sarah Reale, and school board members Andrew Edtl and Oscar Mata. Among the 33 contested races, endorsees won or are leading in 28.

Republican endorsees

  • House District 27: Democrat Liz Oates received 6,762 votes (62.2%) to Loubet’s 4,117 (37.8%). Oates leads by 2,645 votes.
  • House District 38: Unaffiliated candidate Sergio Sotelo received 6,045 votes (55.5%) to McConnehey’s 4,852 (44.5%).
  • Salt Lake County Council District 3: Democrat Luke Maynes received 30,761 votes (58.4%) to Bird’s 21,871 (41.6%).
  • State Board of Education District 8: Democrat Araueni Oliveres received 30,265 votes (53.3%) to McDermott’s 26,547 (46.7%).

The Oates and Maynes races drew the most criticism of Equality Utah’s endorsements. QSaltLake reported earlier that both won, and their margins have grown as more ballots were counted.

Buss trails in Senate District 11

Sen. Emily Buss, a Forward Party member who is friendly to the LGBTQ community, is trailing Republican Brooks Benson by 512 votes. Benson has 16,119 votes (50.8%) to her 15,607 (49.2%).

Gov. Spencer Cox chose Buss to fill the seat after Sen. Daniel Thatcher, who also supported LGBTQ rights, resigned. Thatcher left the Republican Party for the Forward Party in 2025 just before announcing his resignation. Buss leads in Salt Lake County with 55.3% of the vote. She trails in Tooele and Utah counties, which keeps Benson ahead overall.

Democratic endorsees

Many endorsed Democrats won by large margins. Sen. Jen Plumb received 84.5% of the vote in Senate District 9. Rep. Grant Miller received 89.6% in House District 24.

Several races were much closer, and four of them unseated Republican incumbents:

  • Angela Choberka (HD 9) leads Rep. Jake Sawyer by 822 votes.
  • Blake Townsend (HD 36) leads Rep. Jim Dunnigan by 928 votes.
  • Drew Howells (HD 39) leads Rep. Ken Ivory by 1,959 votes.
  • Michael Finch (HD 26) leads Rep. Matt MacPherson by 3,051 votes.

All of the ousted incumbents received F grades for Equal Rights from the Alliance for a Better Utah.

Unaffiliated candidate Patrick Belmont, also endorsed by the PAC, leads Republican incumbent Rep. Jason Thompson by 2,008 votes in House District 3. Celeste Johnson leads Republican Luke Searle by 322 votes in House District 59.

In Senate District 5, which covers parts of Davis, Morgan and Weber counties, Democrat CJ Hernandez leads Republican Jill Koford, 55.8% to 44.2%, a margin of 3,578 votes. No Democrat from outside Salt Lake County has served in the Utah Senate in at least two decades.

Equality Utah hasn’t yet commented on the individual outcomes of its endorsees, but did note voters’ rejection of Amendment B as a positive. They did thank anyone who made the progress possible.

“Let’s make these wins count. Whether you donated, volunteered, knocked on doors, talked with a neighbor, or cast your ballot: thank you,” chair Max Green wrote. “We’ll celebrate the wins, take an honest look at what we can do better, and keep showing up.”
